questions.question: Why is stress (not force) compared with strain when characterising a material?
questions.solution: Force depends on how THICK the sample is — a fat wire needs more force for the same stretch, so force isn't a material property. Stress (F/A) normalises by geometry; strain (ΔL/L) normalises by length. Stress–strain describes the MATERIAL itself; force–extension describes only that particular wire.

questions.question: Steel has a much larger Young's modulus than rubber, yet rubber stretches far more. Resolve the apparent paradox.
questions.solution: Young's modulus Y = stress/strain measures STIFFNESS — resistance to stretch. Steel's huge Y means tiny strain under big stress; rubber's small Y means large strain under small stress. Rubber stretches more because it is LESS stiff, exactly consistent with its smaller Y. 'Stretches more' and 'stiffer' are opposite directions.

questions.concept: Elastic limit vs yield vs breaking
questions.question: On a stress–strain curve, distinguish the proportional limit, elastic limit and breaking point. What happens to a wire stressed between the proportional limit and elastic limit?
questions.solution: Proportional limit: Hooke's law (straight line) ends. Elastic limit: the maximum stress from which the wire still returns to original length — beyond it, permanent (plastic) deformation begins even though the wire hasn't broken. Breaking point: fracture. Stressed between the two limits, the wire deforms permanently but does not snap — it comes back LONGER, not to original length.

questions.question: Why is the energy stored in a stretched wire ½FΔL and not FΔL?
questions.solution: The force grows from 0 to F as the wire stretches — the average force during extension is F/2, so work done = ½FΔL (the area under the F–ΔL graph). FΔL would be the work of a FULL force applied throughout, which is not what happens. The triangular area is the stored elastic PE.

questions.question: When a rubber band is stretched, it gets thinner. What is this behaviour called, and what does a Poisson's ratio near 0.5 imply about the material?
questions.solution: Lateral contraction accompanying longitudinal extension is measured by Poisson's ratio σ = −(lateral strain)/(longitudinal strain). σ ≈ 0.5 means the material's VOLUME stays nearly constant during deformation — it deforms by reshaping, not compressing (rubber behaves this way; most metals ~0.3).
